full_judgment:
2. Respondents as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case 2 of 2011 in the Court of Joint District Judge, Court No. 2, Magura for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 3. The case of the pre-emptor, is that, the pre-emptor himself is a co-sharer in 8(eight) annas share in SA khatian 305 appertaining to Borovila Mouja. His father was owner in possession in SA plots 1203, 1204, 1205, 1272, 1365 of Purbasreekol Mouja and in SA plots 3603, 4072, 4077, 8177 of Sreekol Mouja and in SA plots 81, 83, 120, 323, 405 of Borovila Mouja. He died leaving behind 2(two) sons named Safiuddin Mridha and Golam Sarwar. Thus the pre-emptor is a recorded tenant in plot 119 of SA khatian 305 and heir of other plots. The son and daughters of Golam Sarwar sold the case land in favour of opposite party 1 by the impugned documents dated 14-12-2010 beyond the knowledge of the pre-emptor. The pre-emptor came to learn about the sale from the husband of opposite party 1 on 17-12-2010 and got definite knowledge on 30-12-2010 after getting the certified copy. It is further stated that the pre-emptor and his brother purchased the land of SA plot 405 appertaining to SA khatian 280 by kabala dated 16-2-1972. Their father Bazlur Rahman sold the land of plot 323 of SA khatian 351 to Jamanat Ali through kabala dated 24-10-1962. Subsequently the land was purchased by pre-emptor and his brother from Jamanat Ali Molla by kabala dated 4-2-1971. Although Bazlur Rahman sold 20 decimals of land out of 41 decimals from plot 8171 of SA khatian 1180 but he had right, title, interest and possession in the remaining land. Their mother 365 also had title in plot 1262/21365 SA khatian 1647. Besides the pre-emptor is also an heir. in SA khatian 415. Thus the pre-emptor is the co-sharer by inheritance and purchase. The quantum of land owned by the pre-emptor does not exceed the ceiling. Hence the case for pre-emption was filed. 

 14. Husband of the purchaser as OPW 1 stated in examination-in-chief that opposite parties 2-6 requested pre-emptor to purchase the land. But pre-emptor expressed his inability for want of money and told to sell elsewhere. Opposite parties 2-6 then assigned pre-emptor to sell and pre-emptor then asked opposite party 1 to purchase the land. It was not that pre-emptor did not know the sale and he did not negotiate the sale. In cross he stated that first talk of the sale was held in the house of his neighbor Monwar Khan. Pre-emptor, Monwar Khan, Akter Lasker, OPW 1 were present there Anisuzzaman came when he was informed. The case of involvement and mediation of pre-emptor as made out by opposite party 1 in her pleading and evidence was not at all denied by the pre-emptor. OPW 2 Anisuzzaman who is one of the vendors and nephew of the pre-emptor stated in his deposition that he told his uncle about sale but he refused to purchase for want of money and asked to sell elsewhere. His uncle decided to sell to Mostafa Master. Pre-emptor was present at the time of payment. In cross he stated that talk of sale was held in the house of Monwar Khan and his uncle went to the registry office before him. In the case of Abdus Sobhan Sheikh vs Kazi Jabedullah, 52 DLR 289 it was held that the presence of the pre-emptor in sub-registry office does not amount to acquiescence. We do not agree to this point of view in the present case because pre-emptor's negotiation and presence in the registry office are not challenged and denied in his pleading and evidence. Pre-emptor claims that he had no knowledge about the sale but he did not deny his presence in the registry office. It implies that he had knowledge and took a leading part in bringing about the transaction. In the case of Fazaruddin vs Maizuddin, 1994 BLD (AD) 29 = 44 DLR (AD) 62 it was held that presence of pre-emptor in the registry office does not help pre-emptee to resist pre-emption because in that case pre-emptor went to the registry office to put up resistance to the execution of the impugned sale thus the pre-emptor did not waive his right to preempt. But here in this case pre-emptor went to registry office to encourage execution and his presence in the office is not otherwise challenged or denied by him. OPW 3 stated in examination-in-chief that he was present at the time of talk of the sale. Pre-emptor was also present and fixed the bargain and in cross his statement became more emphatic like OPWs 1 and 2. PTWs 1 and 2 did not make out any case of refusing mediation and even if any evidence had been led to that effect the same would not have borne any importance being beyond pleading. 

 15. It should be a moral trait of people to keep their word or promise. People's trust is broken if they don't keep their word. It creates disorder and confusion in the family and society. In the instant case the previous act and negotiation of the pre-emptor in assisting and encouraging the sale is proved in evidence. Pre-emptor by his act and conduct induced pre-emptee to purchase the case land and having been so induced pre-emptee altered her position and purchased the land. The right of pre-emption inheres in a co-sharer and is flexible' or amenable to be waived or relinquished by consent, conduct or acquiescence even before the sale actually takes effect. Waiver depends upon consent and the fact that the other party has acted upon it is sufficient consideration. Acquiescence implies that a person abstains from interfering while a violation of his legal right is in progress and it operates by way of estoppel. Estoppel is a complex legal notion and very generic and amorphous rule in the law of evidence. It means one cannot contradict, deny or declare one's previous statement made by him to be false. It means to stop. According to it when any person says one thing at one time and another thing at another time then he is prevented from doing so.
